newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMI head takes middle road in euro council dispute.
newsitem.headline: EMI head takes middle road in euro council dispute.

text.p: EMI President Alexandre Lamfalussy has joined the heated debate on the merits of an economic council for the euro zone, but his hopes for a benign forum benefiting monetarists and politicians alike are unlikely to win over Germany's fiercely independent Bundesbank.

In a loose echo of recent proposals by French politicians, Lamfalussy suggested that informal meetings between the future European Central Bank (ECB) and a restricted group of finance ministers could work to both sides' advantage.

Such proposals have outraged the German central bank, whose president Hans Tietmeyer made a rare foray into the French language this month to challenge any attempt to exert "pouvoir politique" (political power) over "pouvoir monetaire" (monetary power).

"The Bundesbank will never ever accept any council which threatens to try and exert influence over monetary policy," said BHF Bank chief economist Hermann Remsperger, a close observer of Bundesbank strategies.

Speaking to journalists late on Monday, Lamfalussy said informal talks with finance ministers only representing the Euro zone would not necessarily undermine the ECB, whose independence was firmly enshrined in the Maastricht Treaty.

"There is a need for an organised dialogue between the governments and the European Central Bank," said Lamfalussy, who later this year ends his term as president of the European Monetary Institute, the forerunner to the ECB.

The EMI head added: "We cannot play with central bank independence. If the objective (of a council) is as a means of influencing the central bank, then I would say no. But if this is a way of organising dialogue, then it would be useful."

The comments, which Lamfalussy said were a personal view and did not represent the views of the EMI council, come at a time when serious differences appear to be taking hold on the economic council issue between France and Germany, or at least between France and the mistrusting Bundesbank.

French officials are playing down the controversy and say it is perfectly reasonable for countries who share the same currency to get together to co-ordinate policies, a move similar to the Group of Seven (G7) forum.

Bonn has so far played a minor role in the debate but state secretary for finance Juergen Stark said on Monday that an economic council could be an informal arrangement for ministers to discuss issues of convergence in the euro zone, and that there was no need to formalise its activities.

Meanwhile Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker, speaking Monday at a meeting of EU finance ministers, said: "There is no reason at all to become nervous (about an economic council). I can't see any reasons for a row at all."
But the Bundesbank's Tietmeyer has warned that setting up a council with power to influence monetary policy would run counter to the Maastricht Treaty.
"I hope that this will ultimately also be seen this way even in countries that do not have a similarly long tradition of an independent central bank," he said in a recent speech.

BHF Bank's Remsperger said the Bundesbank was, in his view justifiably, becoming increasingly nervous that politicians will try to exert their influence to sway the European Central Bank from its mandate -- maintaining price stability.

There was an ever-more apparent gulf between the French view of monetary policy as an element of politics in general, and the German attitude,which sees monetary policy as a separate entity partly due to a history of dramatic inflation.
"It is worrying that these differences are becoming more and more obvious as the deadline for convergence in the euro area gets closer," Remsperger said.
Remsperger said the German government was likely to be just as reluctant as the Bundesbank to bow to suggestions that political weight could be exerted on the ECB.
"I do not believe there can be any differences between Bonn and Frankfurt on this point," he said.
